summary: Fiji is one of the most open countries in the Pacific: citizens of more than a hundred countries — the whole EU, the UK, the US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, most of the Commonwealth and every Pacific Islands Forum neighbor — receive a free four-month visitor permit on arrival, while everyone else must apply to the Fiji Immigration Department before traveling.

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months beyond the date you intend to leave Fiji. This is enforced by airlines at check-in as well as by immigration.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP)
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required from travelers aged 1 and over arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, which for most visitors only matters if the trip routes through South America or Africa. No vaccination is required for arrivals from Australia, New Zealand, Asia, North America or Europe.

travelInsurance.text: Fiji does not require travel insurance for entry and nothing is checked at the border. Treat claims that it is mandatory with suspicion. It is nevertheless the single most useful thing to buy: hospitals in Suva, Lautoka and Nadi handle most emergencies, but anything serious means an air ambulance to Australia or New Zealand costing tens of thousands of dollars. If you plan to dive, check that diving and hyperbaric treatment are covered.

onwardTicket.text: Visitors must hold a confirmed onward or return ticket and be able to name where they are staying — both are conditions of the visitor permit granted on arrival, and airlines check the ticket before boarding.

proofOfFunds.text: Visitors are expected to show sufficient funds to support themselves without working. A card statement or cash is enough. No fixed figure is published, and in practice officers only ask when the stay is long or the itinerary is vague.

declarations.name: Fiji Arrival Card and Biosecurity Declaration
declarations.text: Every passenger completes an arrival card that doubles as a customs and biosecurity declaration, handed out on the aircraft. Fiji's biosecurity rules are strict — food, seeds, plants, wooden carvings, and used camping, hiking or diving gear must all be declared, and undeclared items attract on-the-spot fines.

currencyLimits.text: Amounts of FJD 10,000 or more in cash (or the foreign-currency equivalent) must be declared to Customs on arrival and departure.

source.name: Fiji Revenue and Customs — traveller information

notes: Biosecurity is taken seriously: declare all food, plant material, seeds, wooden items and used outdoor equipment — hiking boots and dive gear are inspected and may be cleaned before release.
Bringing kava into Fiji is unrestricted in practice, but taking it out is limited by the rules of the country you are heading to — Australia and New Zealand both cap personal quantities.
Firearms, ammunition and drone imports require prior approval; recreational drones also need clearance from the Civil Aviation Authority of Fiji for anything beyond casual use.

payments.text: Resorts, hotels, tour operators and supermarkets in Nadi, Denarau, Suva and Lautoka take cards, and ATMs are easy to find in the towns. Once you reach the Yasawas, Lomaiviti or a village stay it turns cash-only — draw Fijian dollars before you leave the mainland, and keep small notes for buses, markets and the kava you present as sevusevu.

safety.text: Fiji is a relaxed and welcoming destination with little violent crime against visitors, though opportunistic theft from hotel rooms, beaches and rental cars happens and Suva and Nadi warrant normal city caution after dark. The genuine risks are environmental: cyclones between November and April, strong reef currents and rips, and the distance to advanced medical care.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Fiji travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: May to October is the dry season — lower humidity, clear water for diving and no cyclone risk. November to April is hotter and wetter, with the cyclone season running roughly November 1 to April 30; it is also cheaper and greener.

idp.text: Fiji is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Fiji yet.

tips.text: Cyclone season runs from November to April, and a severe cyclone can close airports and ferry routes for days. Traveling in those months, book flexible fares, keep the Fiji Meteorological Service forecast in view, and make sure your insurance covers weather cancellation rather than only medical costs.

Serious illness or injury means evacuation to Australia or New Zealand. There is no comprehensive tertiary hospital in Fiji, and the country's only recompression chamber is in Suva, hours from the outer islands. Hold insurance with medical evacuation coverage and, if diving, check the policy names hyperbaric treatment.

Visiting a village is a formal occasion: bring a bundle of kava root as sevusevu for the chief, cover your shoulders and knees, take off your hat and sunglasses, and remove your shoes before entering a house. Ask before photographing people.

The permit granted on arrival to visa-exempt visitors is four months, not the 30 or 90 days most countries give — unusually generous. It can be extended, but total visitor time is capped at six months in any twelve, and extensions must be applied for at an Immigration office before the current permit expires.

Reef passages produce strong outgoing currents, and stonefish and cone shells sit on the shallow flats. Swim where the resort points you, wear reef shoes when walking on coral, and check tides before crossing a lagoon on foot.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Fiji?
faq.answer: Probably not. More than a hundred nationalities — all EU and EEA states, the UK, Ireland, the US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, India, most Commonwealth countries and every Pacific Islands Forum neighbor — get a free visitor permit stamped on arrival for up to four months. If your country is not on that list you must apply to the Fiji Immigration Department before you travel; there is no visa on arrival for non-exempt nationalities.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Fiji?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt visitors are normally granted four months on arrival. That can be extended in further blocks at an Immigration office, but the total visitor stay is limited to six months within any twelve-month period, after which you need a different permit category.

faq.question: What do I need to show at Fijian immigration?
faq.answer: A passport valid for at least six months beyond your departure, a confirmed onward or return ticket, the address of your first accommodation, and a completed arrival card with the biosecurity declaration. Officers may also ask how you will fund the stay.

faq.question: Is travel insurance mandatory for Fiji?
faq.answer: No. Fiji does not require insurance for entry and nothing is checked at the border. Buy it anyway for the medical evacuation coverage. The nearest advanced hospitals are in Australia and New Zealand, and an air ambulance from Nadi runs into tens of thousands of dollars.

faq.question: When is cyclone season in Fiji and should I avoid it?
faq.answer: Roughly November 1 to April 30. Most trips in those months pass without incident and prices are lower, but a severe cyclone can shut airports and inter-island ferries for several days. If you travel then, choose flexible tickets and insurance that covers weather disruption.

faq.question: Do I need anything extra to visit the outer islands?
faq.answer: No separate permit — your entry stamp covers the whole country, including the Yasawa, Mamanuca and Lau groups. What you do need is planning: boat and light-aircraft schedules are sparse, many islands are cash-only, and the Lau group in particular can be days apart from a scheduled service.
